Hello. I'm relatively new to Lean. Played with it a bit a few years ago, but trying to use it seriously now.
My research for my degree was about infinite volume quantum lattice systems, and so I thought it would be nice to have a definitions for those in Lean, or at least for uniformly hyperfinite algebras.
So, I'm starting to work towards formalizing UHF algebras using mathlib, hoping to eventually get it to the quality where I could contribute it to mathlib, and I'd especially appreciate some early feedback on whether the approach I'm taking is the right approach.

As a first step, I defined the "amplification" map A∈Mn(C)↦A⊗IkA \in M_n(\mathbb{C}) \mapsto A \otimes I_k A∈Mn​(C)↦A⊗Ik​ (where IkI_kIk​ is the identity operator in Mk(C)M_k(\mathbb{C})Mk​(C)) as a StarAlgHom:

noncomputable def amplify
  (n k : Type*)
  [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n]
  [Fintype k] [DecidableEq k] :
  Matrix n n ℂ →⋆ₐ[ℂ] Matrix (n × k) (n × k) ℂ := by
    sorry  -- details snipped for brevity, on request I can edit them in

using Matrix.kroneckerStarAlgEquiv n k ℂ and Algebra.TensorProduct.includeLeft.
I also defined a amplify_apply lemma and a compatibility lemma showing that iterated amplification is equivalent to amplification with a larger set, using Matrix.kronecker_assoc :

-- This currently casts to algebra maps, not star algebra maps. Something to fix.
lemma amplify_assoc
  (n k k2 : Type*) [Fintype n] [DecidableEq n] [Fintype k] [DecidableEq k]
  [Fintype k2] [DecidableEq k2] :
  ((Matrix.reindexAlgEquiv ℂ ℂ (Equiv.prodAssoc n k k2)).toAlgHom).comp
    (((amplify (n × k) k2).comp (amplify n k)).toAlgHom) =
  (amplify n (k × k2)).toAlgHom := by
  ext A
  have h := Matrix.kronecker_assoc A (1 : Matrix k k ℂ) (1 : Matrix k2 k2 ℂ)
  simp [amplify_apply, h]

I have a few design questions about this setup:
1) In my definition for amplify, I currently need some letI statements for typeclass inference (namely. Semiring / Algebra instances on tensor products) to get the definition for amplify to work (to get Semiring ((Matrix n n ℂ) ⊗[ℂ] (Matrix k k ℂ)) and Algebra ℂ ((Matrix n n ℂ) ⊗[ℂ] (Matrix k k ℂ)) from Algebra.TensorProduct.instSemiring and Algebra.TensorProduct.instAlgebra respectively.)
Is there a more idiomatic way to structure this so that these letI parts are unnecessary?
2) Is it better to define this map using the kind of tensor product used by Algebra.TensorProduct.includeLeft, ( ⊗[ℂ] one), or should I stick entirely on the Kronecker products of matrices side?
3) Should I generalize to using 𝕜 with [RCLike 𝕜] already, or is it ok to stick to ℂ for now, and generalize the code once I have more written?
(I suppose none of what I have so far particularly depends on it being ℂ, as I'm not yet using any analytic properties, and I guess at this point any field equipped with a star operation would work, but, when I get to the limits / closure of union of sub $C^*$-algebras, I'll need the analytic properties.)

(For transparency: I have been using a little bit of LLM-based assistance (getting some advice and explanations from ChatGPT, and a tad from the autocomplete in VSCode), but I'd be willing to stop using these if preferred.)

My tentative plan is to define a UHF algebra as a C∗C^*C∗-algebra equipped with a sequence (or directed system) of matrix algebras with compatible embeddings, such that the closure of the union of their images is the whole algebra (rather than using an abstract inductive limit).

More broadly, does this seem like a reasonable starting point for working towards defining UHF algebras (and maybe later infinite volume quantum lattice systems)?
I'd really appreciate any feedback on whether this is the "right" approach before I build more on top of it.

Since my original post, I’ve made some progress on the setup (defining reindexStarAlgEquiv, fixing amplify_assoc to use StarAlgHoms, and sketching structures for directed systems of CStarAlgebras and their colimits).

At this point, the main thing I’m unsure about is how to structure the directed system in a way that aligns with mathlib conventions.

Concretely, suppose I want a directed system of CStarAlgebras with StarAlgHoms as the maps. There seem to be a few reasonable approaches:

  1. define a new structure mirroring DirectedSystem, but with StarAlgHoms, together with a lemma relating it to DirectedSystem,
  2. define a structure or class extending DirectedSystem with additional fields,
  3. define a structure that contains a DirectedSystem as a field and builds on top of it.

All of these "work", but I’m not sure which pattern would be preferred for mathlib.

Would anyone be able to advise on which approach is more idiomatic?

(Happy to share code if helpful.)

I have opinions based on looking at some parts of Mathlib and a lot of posts on this Zulip. I am not a maintainer nor a contributor, nor have I any expertise in hyperfinite algebras, uniform or otherwise. So consider the following more as an attempt to help guide than as gospel.

My take is that Mathlib is intended to handle as large a population of users as they can. While "user" often means person studying a particular area or theory of mathematics, here I mean theory or area by "user". Much work is put into taking a particular structure for the proof of a theorem (or of a class of models which are the subject of such proofs) and generalizing that proof to apply as widely as possible. This is apparent when looking at results in number theory: some of them apply to algebraic structures which share some of the properties of the integers or even natural numbers.

If Mathlib has a niche which includes hyperfinite algebras, then it helps the effort if that niche is filled in with theorems or counterexamples applying to as many hyperfinite algebras as possible, or at least delineating which structures/examples apply to which widely used portion of algebras. That way the path for work which builds on this becomes clear.

Possibly all hyperfinite algebras are uniform, I don't know. (Nor do I know if there is a hyperfinite algebra niche in Mathlib.) However, many of the operations/systems you are building can be generalized to a larger family of structures. So I recommend the following:

a) find someone who is expert at Lean and has seen the field in which you work, and ask them if they have seen anything like your proposal.
b) use tools like loogle or Leansearch to see if anything resembling what you are developing appears in mathlib or associated repositories. Here the resemblance can be pretty weak: for example you might find "directed system" defined on elements in a partial order , and that someone extended this to commutative monoid or some other structure. See if you can use this code directly, and if not, refer to the inspirational code in a 'docstring', which may suggest to a maintainer that the inspirational code can be extended.
c) continue your own development, where you try (initial attempts at) all of your approaches specifically for UHF algebras, with an eye toward documenting which parts of your system are specifically toward your desired theory/application, and which parts are for more general situations.
d) iterate a) b) and c) as desired.

(I don't think any of the ideas you suggest are wrong. However, if your primary goal is to get into Mathlib rather than developing your own useful repository, I suspect none of them is "right". So change the primary goal perhaps?)

You may end up with none of your code getting in Mathlib, but your ideas for structure and systematizing may be added for you if you communicate them well in your work. If you document well, they may even spell your name right.

Reminder: this is based more on opinion, with some experience coming from outside this Zulip/domain.

content:
Thanks, I really appreciate you taking the time to write this, it's very helpful.

Your point about mathlib aiming to handle results in a rather general way matches with what I've seen so far.

As for "(non-uniformly) hyperfinite algebras", I think these are usually called "approximately finite dimensional algebras" rather than "hyperfinite", but yeah, what I have for the directed systems should work for those as well I think? I'll try to keep that general use case in mind.
Your suggestion to separate out what is UHF specific from what should be more general is helpful, and I'll try to keep it in mind.

One thing I'm still trying to get a feel for is how early to generalize, whether to first get something working in the specific case I have in mind and then try to make it handle more cases, or to try to build at the right/highest level of generality from the start. (e.g. in the amplify method I mentioned in my first post, I initially had it over ℂ, but have since replaced that with being over 𝕜 with [RCLike 𝕜])

That's a great suggestion to use those search tools to try to find other things building on directed systems, to see how they approached it. I haven't used loogle or Leanseach much yet, but I'll definitely try them for this.

Thank you again for your suggestions.
I'll try to comment on this in the next few days. I'm posting here so it shows up in my feed of conversations in which I've participated so that I remember to do so.
Oh wow, yeah, I hadn't realized there was Mathlib/Algebra/Colimit/DirectLimit.lean , and that will definitely be a file for me to take a close look at and learn from, and probably use.

(e.g. in the amplify method I mentioned in my first post, I initially had it over ℂ, but have since replaced that with being over 𝕜 with [RCLike 𝕜])

TL;DR: Try everything but misformalization, and document/adapt as you go.

You will develop your workflow to suit you and your comfort level and level of understanding. You might sacrifice some level of comfort, but don't sacrifice your level of understanding. What this might mean in terms of your workflow:

Have your first example developed over the complexes, and do small increments on that example, all the while maintaining the ability to compile (be "Lean-good") and be machine-understandable (the definitions "say what you mean", so that your idea "matches the idea the machine" has; IOW avoid misformalization). Then switch to the version over arbitrary field k and see that the version with k tracks with your version over C, and compiles and is machine-understandable. (How often you switch and how big the increments are between switching is up to you; my suggestion is switch often and step smaller until your understanding of both examples (and perhaps other future development) is as rock-solid as you can make it.)

As you do this, see which parts use which properties of C, and ensure that you use the same properties over k. Keep a TODO: type comment available to indicate possibilities for generalization, or remarks that indicate difficulties or requirements that might inhibit generalization. (You might develop some scripts or setup that later extracts the comments into a side file for individual study).

Similarly, you can develop several approaches in parallel (or serial, if you think you can streamline a second approach by finding many of the issues in the first approach), again documenting what assumptions you need and what parts you can generalize. When two or more of your approaches rely on the same kind of structured argument or the same method, see if that method can be pulled out into its own file so that you can refactor your approaches, each depending on this common subset.

Read some blogs/books on software engineering and systems design. Don't consider their mantras as gospel: there will be times where repeating yourself or your code will be convenient, and your naming convention can differ from naming conventions in professional coding. However, there are many good ideas for mathematical development present and tested in these disciplines, and adopting some of the ideas will help you develop your workflow.

Above all, make sure each small step compiles and formalizes well. Use #check, #eval, and other diagnostic tools often, so that you understand that the machine "understands" what you are telling it to understand. Consider steps toward meta-programming, which might be as simple as writing a side script or macros to automate common steps in your workflow, and in your workflow log, write down why you wrote such script or macro.

Good luck, and good work.

content:
Thanks again for the earlier feedback — it was very helpful. After reading Mathlib/Algebra/Colimit/DirectLimit.lean, I reworked my approach to better match mathlib style.

I’ve shifted focus from defining UHF algebras directly to first developing general direct limits of directed systems of C∗C^*C∗-algebras, with UHF algebras and quantum spin systems as later applications.

So far, I’ve implemented instances on DirectLimit G f for:

  • Star, InvolutiveStar, StarMul, StarAddMonoid, StarRing, StarModule
  • Algebra

following the pattern in DirectLimit.lean, assuming the maps f lie in appropriate homclasses.

I then started extending this to normed structures. For Norm, I ran into the issue that there doesn’t seem to be a homclass expressing “norm-preserving maps” (in contrast to the algebraic cases). I worked around this by adding explicit hypotheses that the maps preserve norms, but this feels less clean.

Would it be appropriate to introduce a homclass for norm-presing maps here, or is there an existing pattern in mathlib I should be following instead?

With the current setup, I’ve also obtained instances of:

  • NormedAddGroup, NormedAddCommGroup
  • NonUnitalNormedRing, CStarRing

(so far without the completion step; handling completion and the universal property for it is my next goal).

Does it sound reasonable to start by PR-ing the reusable direct-limit instances for the Star hierarchy (and possibly Algebra) in small pieces, and leave the normed / C∗C^*C∗ aspects for possible future PRs?

Matthew Corbelli said:

Does it sound reasonable to start by PR-ing the reusable direct-limit instances for the Star hierarchy (and possibly Algebra) in small pieces, and leave the normed / C∗C^*C∗ aspects for possible future PRs?

Yes, please do.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Yes, please do.

Alright, will do, thanks!

The instances for those classes (the ones involving Star) for the DirectLimit, require an additional import of Mathlib.Algebra.Star.StarRingHom beyond what is currently used in Mathlib.Algebra.Colimit.DirectLimit.

Would you prefer I:

  1. add these instances (and a few associated lemmas) to Mathlib.Algebra.Colimit.DirectLimit, introducing that extra import, or
  2. put them in a new file extending it?

Thanks again.
